$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\operatorname{cot}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{6}\int \operatorname{csc}⁡u\operatorname{cot}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{5}{6}\operatorname{csc}⁡(6x+\frac{\pi }{3})+C\end{aligned}

Let $u = x^3 - \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u = x^2\,\textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\cdot \frac{1}{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {sec}^{2}⁡(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})+C\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Evaluate the integral $$
\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\tan x \sec^2 x}{1+\tan^2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(1+\tan^2 x) = 2\tan{x}\sec^2 x.
$$

So, let $u = 1+\tan^2 x.$ Differentiating, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2\tan x\sec^2 x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \tan x\sec^2 x\,\textrm d x.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\pi/4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $2$ |

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{1+{tan}^{2}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that if we let $u = x^2,$ then we have

$$
\int \underbrace{2x}_{u'} \cos({\overbrace{x^2}^u})\,\textrm d x.
$$

In other words, the factor multiplying the trigonometric function is the derivative of the argument! Integrals like this can always be solved using substitution.

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d u = 2x\,\textrm d x.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\cdot 2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{2}+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x \\ \text{d}u & =2x\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u & =x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^2+1.$

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline x & -1 & 0 \\ \hline u & 2 & 1 \\ \hline\end{array}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^0 x(x^2+1)^3\,\textrm{d}x=\int_2^1 u^3\,\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{1}{u}^{3}\,\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2}^{1}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{4}}{4}{|}_{2}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{1}^{4}-{2}^{4}}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1-16}{4} \\  & =-\frac{15}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Important**: Note that in this example, when we changed the limits the integral $$
\displaystyle \int_{-1}^0 \ldots \textrm{d}x
$$ became $$
\displaystyle \int_{2}^1 \ldots \textrm{d}u.
$$ When changing the limits, it is important to respect the order in which the limits are applied. The lower limit of the integral in $u$ must correspond to the lower limit of the integral in $x.$ Same for the upper limit.

We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & ={x}^{3}+2 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2} \\ \text{d}u & =3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & ={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^3+2.$

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline x & -1 & 2 \\ \hline u & 1 & 10 \\ \hline\end{array}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
\int_{-1}^2 \dfrac{1}{(x^3+2)}\,x^2\textrm{d}x=\int_1^{10} \dfrac{1}{u}\,\cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{10}\frac{1}{u}\,\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{10}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{1}^{10} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(10)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(10).\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Calculate the integral $$
\displaystyle{\int} (2\sec^2 x + \sec x \tan x )\, \textrm{d}x.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that 

$$
\int \sec^2 x \, \textrm dx = \tan x + C
$$

and

$$
\int \sec x \tan x \, \textrm dx = \sec x + C.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
		\int (2\sec^2 x + \sec x \tan x )\, \textrm{d}x& = 2 \int \sec^2 x \, \textrm{d}x+ \int \sec x \tan x \, \textrm{d}x \\
										&=2\tan x + \sec x + C.

\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that 

$$
\int \csc^2 x \, \textrm dx = -\cot x + C
$$

and

$$
\int \csc x \cot x \, \textrm dx = -\csc x + C.
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int csc⁡x(csc⁡x+3cot⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡x+3csc⁡xcot⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x+3\int csc⁡xcot⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-cot⁡x-3csc⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$
